newsitem.title: CHINA: Beijing residents shocked, saddened by Deng's death.
newsitem.headline: Beijing residents shocked, saddened by Deng's death.

text.p: Residents of China's capital voiced emotions ranging from shock and sadness to cold indifference after waking on Thursday morning to news of the death of paramount leader Deng Xiaoping.

Tighter security and the bright red national flag flying at half-mast in Tiananmen Square were the only hints of a break from routine after the early morning announcement that the greatest communist reformer of the 20th century was dead.

Police, some carrying assault rifles, stood guard at the end of the nearby lane in central Beijing where Deng had lived and patrolled the lanes around the Zhongnanhai government compound near the Forbidden City, abode of China's emperors.
Deng, mastermind of 18 years of reform that turned China into an economic powerhouse, died in an advanced stage of Parkinson's disease late on Wednesday. He was 92.
Some were shocked at Deng's demise. Others were saddened.
"My first reaction is great shock," said Liu Hongxin, a 21-year-old student waiting for a train in the pre-dawn chill at Beijing's main railway station.
"I feel a great sadness," said snack vendor Xie Weicai as he prepared his pavement stove for the morning's business, but his regret was not universal among the capital's residents.
"The emperor is dead," Yang Feng'in said and broke into laughter when asked if he had listened to radio broadcasts and was aware Deng had died.
"He has been inactive in politics for so long. If you didn't mention him, I would have thought he was dead," said Yang, a truck driver laid off recently from a loss-making state firm.

It was business as usual on the capital's streets, with residents busy manning shops and crowding on to buses, a scene in stark contrast to the paralysis that gripped China with the passing of Chairman Mao Zedong in September 1976.
In Tiananmen Square, residents and visitors gathered to see the dawn raising of China's red flag emblazoned with five gold stars.
Plainclothes police stopped at least two people from laying wreaths at a monument in the square, eyewitnesses said.

University students have in the past smashed bottles to vent their anger at Deng, whose name rhymes with the Chinese for "little bottle". Deng ordered the military to crush student-led demonstrations for democracy in June 1989, resulting in heavy loss of life.

But there were no reports of bottle-smashing or displays of protest posters in the university area of western Beijing on Thursday. Most students have yet to return from Lunar New Year holidays. A taxi driver surnamed Zhao said he wept when Mao died in 1976 but shed no tears over Deng's departure.
"We were ideologically naive then... The values of people are now different," Zhao said.

"In the past, it didn't matter if food was not good so long as there was enough. It was all for Mao Zedong. It was all for socialism," he said, pointing to a picture of Mao alongside a statue of Buddha on his dashboard.
Many said it was unfortunate that Deng had not lived to see the July 1 handover of Hong Kong -- a British colony for more than 150 years -- that Deng had helped to bring about.
"My greatest regret is that Deng Xiaoping will not be able to see China resuming sovereignty over Hong Kong," Zhao said.
